title: Research with Evidence
summary: After this intermediate module, learners can turn a research question into a scoped claim, connect that claim to appropriate evidence, and communicate conclusions without overstating what the evidence supports. Learners will also be able to create an evidence record that another person can audit.
objectives: Distinguish a source's reported evidence from an inference drawn from that evidence.
Select evidence that matches the subject, conditions, and scope of a claim.
Record a claim, its supporting evidence, its source, its scope, and its limitations.
Revise an unsupported or overly broad conclusion into a claim that the cited evidence supports.
Explain which source changed in this update and which parts of the module the correction affected.

sections.title: Source correction
paragraphs: The prior source entry was content/modules/ai-foundations/research-with-evidence.json. The update record identifies it as an internal path from an unregistered publisher that had never been verified. It did not provide the required resolvable HTTPS source.

That source entry has been removed and replaced by canonical arXiv records for Model Cards for Model Reporting, Datasheets for Datasets, and Holistic Evaluation of Language Models. This change affects the module's source provenance and the guidance about documenting context, datasets, evaluation conditions, and limitations. Material unrelated to that correction is unchanged.

sections.title: Level and learning outcome
paragraphs: This is an intermediate-level module. It assumes basic familiarity with reading technical prose and identifying a document's main conclusion. It does not assume prior knowledge of research methodology, statistical testing, or any named AI system.

Before this module, a learner may have treated a citation as sufficient support for a statement. After completing it, the learner can inspect what a source actually reports, separate that evidence from later interpretation, test whether the evidence matches the claim, and write a conclusion with an explicit scope.

sections.title: Separate claims, evidence, and inference
paragraphs: A claim is a statement that could be supported, qualified, or contradicted. Evidence is the relevant material a source reports, such as a described method, dataset, observation, or evaluation result. An inference is the reasoning used to move from that evidence to a conclusion.

Keep these elements separate in your notes. For example, a paper may report results under named evaluation conditions. The reported results are evidence. A conclusion that the same performance will occur under different conditions is an additional inference, not another result from the paper.

A citation identifies a source, but it does not by itself demonstrate that the source supports every part of the surrounding sentence. The researcher must compare the sentence with the source's subject, method, conditions, and stated limitations.
sections.callout: Use the narrowest claim that the available evidence supports. Broaden it only when additional evidence supports the broader scope.

sections.title: Match the source to the claim
paragraphs: Begin with the exact claim you want to support. Identify its subject, asserted outcome, conditions, and scope. Then inspect the original paper or report rather than relying only on a summary of it.

Model Cards for Model Reporting proposes documentation that includes intended uses, evaluation information, relevant factors, and limitations. This supports asking whether evidence was produced for the use and conditions named in a claim.

Datasheets for Datasets proposes documenting matters such as a dataset's motivation, composition, collection process, uses, and maintenance. This supports checking whether conclusions about data account for how the data was created and what it represents.

Holistic Evaluation of Language Models describes evaluation across multiple scenarios and metrics. This supports checking whether a broad performance claim rests on evidence that covers the relevant conditions and measures rather than on one isolated result.

sections.title: Build an auditable evidence record
paragraphs: For each important conclusion, record five elements in plain language: the claim, the evidence, the source, the supported scope, and the limitations. The claim is your proposed statement. The evidence is what the source directly reports. The source is the document containing that evidence. The scope states where the evidence applies. The limitations identify boundaries or unanswered questions.

Include a precise location when the source provides one, such as a section, table, or figure. Preserve enough context to determine what was measured and under which conditions. Do not copy a number into a new claim without also recording what that number describes.
If the source does not establish a required part of the claim, omit that part from the conclusion. Do not replace missing evidence with confident wording.

sections.title: Test the reasoning
paragraphs: First, test relevance. Ask whether the evidence concerns the same subject and outcome as the claim. Second, test scope. Ask whether the evaluated conditions cover the conditions named in the claim. Third, test sufficiency. Ask whether the evidence supports the entire conclusion or only a narrower statement.

Next, look for alternative explanations and documented limitations. A result associated with one factor does not by itself establish that the factor caused the result. Likewise, evidence from one dataset, scenario, or metric does not automatically support a conclusion about every dataset, scenario, or metric.

When evidence supports only a narrower conclusion, revise the wording. Name the evaluated conditions and avoid universal terms such as always, all, or every unless the evidence actually establishes that scope.

sections.title: Use a repeatable workflow
paragraphs: Write the proposed claim before searching. Break it into subject, outcome, conditions, and scope. Decide what evidence would support each part.
Open the original source and identify what it directly reports. Record the method or evaluation context, the relevant result, and any limitation that changes how the result should be interpreted.

Compare the proposed claim with the evidence record. Remove unsupported details, narrow unsupported scope, and distinguish the source's findings from your own inference. If an important part remains unsupported, do not assert it.

Finish by checking that every important factual claim points to a source that readers can open, that the source addresses the claim, and that your wording preserves the source's conditions and limitations.

questions.prompt: A source reports a result under one named evaluation condition. Which conclusion is supported without additional evidence?
choices: The result applies under the reported evaluation condition.
The result applies under every possible condition.
The result proves that the evaluated system is suitable for every use.
The result makes the source's limitations irrelevant.
questions.explanation: The module explains that evidence supports the conditions under which it was produced. Extending the result to every condition or use requires additional evidence.

questions.prompt: Which item is an inference rather than directly reported evidence?
choices: A paper describes the dataset used in an evaluation.
A table reports a result for a named metric.
A researcher concludes that the reported result will also occur under different, unevaluated conditions.
A source states a limitation of its evaluation.
questions.explanation: Extending a reported result to unevaluated conditions is reasoning beyond what the source directly reports, so it is an inference.

questions.prompt: Which evidence record follows the method taught in this module?
choices: A citation with no explanation of what it supports.
A claim, the reported evidence, the source, the supported scope, and the limitations.
A conclusion and a list of unrelated sources.
A copied result with its conditions removed.
questions.explanation: The module defines an auditable evidence record as the claim, evidence, source, supported scope, and limitations.

questions.prompt: What source change triggered this correction?
choices: An unverified internal path was removed and replaced with canonical HTTPS arXiv records.
A named software configuration was changed.
A new prerequisite module was added.
A performance figure was estimated and inserted.
questions.explanation: The update note states that the unverified internal path was removed because it was not a resolvable HTTPS source, and canonical arXiv records now support the affected guidance.
